problemText: A weather forecast on television predicts rain and cooler temperatures for the next three days in your city. What is the forecast describing — the weather or the climate?
choices: The climate, because forecasts predict the permanent atmospheric conditions that define a location over many years
The climate, because it tells you what temperatures and rainfall to expect in that location
The weather, because it describes what the atmosphere will be doing over a few days, not the long-term pattern the city usually has
The weather, because short-term predictions of rain and temperature changes represent conditions in the next few days, which is weather not climate
hints: Remember: does this describe right now or a few days, or does it describe the pattern a place is usually like?
A forecast is a prediction for the near future — is that a short stretch of time or a long-term pattern?

problemText: Mount Iris has a cool, dry climate. On one winter day there, it snows heavily for 12 hours and the temperature stays below freezing. Does this snowy day prove that Mount Iris's climate description is wrong?
choices: Yes, because a single heavy snowfall proves the entire climate classification of dry must be incorrect for that location
No, but only if the snow happened more than one year ago
Yes, because snow indicates wet conditions, which directly contradicts a dry climate classification no matter when it occurs
No, because one snowy day is that day's weather, and it does not change the overall pattern Mount Iris usually has
hints: Can a place with one kind of climate still have a day that does not match it?
Does one day of snow, however heavy, change what the place's climate pattern is year after year?

problemText: A student reads that Grayhaven's climate is warm and humid year-round. The next day, the student sees a news story saying that yesterday was unusually cold and dry in Grayhaven, with frost on the ground. Which statement correctly explains what the student has read?
choices: The climate description and the news story are both correct — they answer two different questions about the same place
The news story is wrong, because Grayhaven's climate is warm and humid, so no day there can be cold and dry
The climate description used to be true, but yesterday's weather proves it has changed
The news story is describing Grayhaven's weather, but the climate description is about a different place with a similar name
hints: Can the same place be truthfully described both ways at once — one way about its climate and one way about its weather?
A climate description answers the question 'What is the pattern?', and weather reporting answers the question 'What is happening right now?'

problemText: A gardener in Northfield reads that Northfield has a moderate, temperate climate. Before planting seeds, the gardener checks a weather report that says 'Frost expected tonight and tomorrow night.' Should the gardener plant the seeds based on the climate description, or should the gardener wait until after checking the weather forecast? Explain why.
choices: The gardener should plant now, because a climate description tells what will happen every single day of the year and frost cannot occur in any location with a moderate, temperate classification
The gardener should wait, because the weather forecast describes what will happen in the next few days, and the climate description does not predict any single day
The gardener should plant now, because a climate description is more accurate than a weather forecast for planning activities on any specific day in the near future
The gardener should wait, but the decision depends on what the climate description says will happen during the exact same dates when frost is forecast
hints: Does knowing a place's climate tell you what the weather will be on any particular day?
The gardener needs a prediction for the next few days — should that come from a climate description or from a weather forecast?

problemText: Two statements are made about City X: (1) 'City X had a rainy week last month,' and (2) 'City X has a dry climate.' A student says these two statements contradict each other and cannot both be true. Explain what mistake the student is making.
choices: The student is right — a place cannot have both a dry climate and rain in any week of the year, so one statement must be false
The student is wrong because the climate classification must change immediately to 'wet' whenever rain falls during any week, making statement 2 outdated
The student is wrong because statement 1 is about weather (a short time) and statement 2 is about climate (the long-term pattern), and both can be true of the same place at once
The student is wrong because weather patterns always match climate classifications exactly, so if one week was rainy, the entire month must have been rainy and the climate cannot be dry
hints: One statement is about one week (a short stretch of time) and the other is about the pattern the place is usually like — which one is weather and which is climate?
Can a place have one kind of climate and still have some days or weeks that do not match that pattern?

problemText: A scientist studying Blackstone Valley collects data on the atmosphere there for 20 years. She finds that the average summer temperature is 23 degrees Celsius, snow falls in winter about 60 percent of the years, and rain falls about evenly across all seasons. A local resident says, 'Last summer we had one month where the temperature never went above 15 degrees Celsius — that month proves the scientist's temperature numbers are wrong.' Is the resident's claim correct? Why or why not?
choices: Yes, one cold month is enough to show that a 20-year average of 23 degrees cannot be right
Yes, but only if that cold month happened in a different year than most of the other data the scientist collected over those 20 years
No, because any month that is colder than the average means the scientist's calculation method was wrong and the true average must be lower

No, because one unusual month is weather for that time period, while the 20-year average describes the climate pattern, and one day or month that differs from the climate pattern does not change what that pattern is
hints: Is one month, no matter how unusual, enough time to describe a place's climate pattern, or is it a short stretch of time called weather?
If a place's climate average is 23 degrees over 20 years, can there still be individual months or days that are much colder or warmer than that?

problemText: Water sitting in an ocean is warmed by energy from the sun and changes into an invisible gas that rises into the air. What is the name of this stage of the water cycle?
choices: Collection
Condensation
Precipitation
Evaporation
hints: This stage happens first, when the sun's energy warms liquid water.
The word contains 'vapor,' and that gas is what forms during this stage.

problemText: A puddle on the playground disappears on a hot, dry afternoon without any person removing the water or the puddle draining away. Which stage of the water cycle is responsible for the puddle vanishing?
choices: Evaporation, because the sun's warmth changed the water into rising invisible vapor
Condensation, because cooling water vapor forms liquid droplets that cluster together in the air
Precipitation, because water is falling from clouds and landing on the ground as rain or snow
Collection, because liquid water is gathering and storing in oceans, lakes, and underground reserves
hints: Look for which stage involves the sun warming liquid water and turning it into a gas.
The puddle is disappearing into the air, not falling from the sky or gathering into a lake.

problemText: High in the sky, water vapor that has risen from the ocean cools as it reaches a higher altitude. The cooled water vapor changes back into countless tiny liquid droplets that cluster together and float in the air. Which stage of the water cycle is being described?
choices: Evaporation, because water is changing from a liquid into an invisible gas that rises into the atmosphere
Condensation, because water vapor is cooling and becoming liquid water droplets
Precipitation, because the liquid droplets have accumulated and are now heavy enough to fall as rain
Collection, because water droplets are merging together and flowing toward rivers and oceans
hints: This stage happens when something cools down and changes from a gas back into a liquid.
The tiny droplets floating together in the air form a cloud, which is the definition of this stage.

problemText: A student observes a lake early in the morning and notices the water level is slightly lower than it was the previous afternoon. Later that same day, a cloud forms above the lake, and by evening, rain falls and raises the lake's level back up. Place the correct stage name on each event: the water level dropping in the morning, the cloud forming during the afternoon, and the rain falling in the evening. Which choice lists all three stages in the correct order?
choices: Evaporation, precipitation, condensation
Condensation, evaporation, precipitation
Evaporation, condensation, precipitation
Precipitation, condensation, evaporation
hints: The water level dropped because warmth from the sun turned liquid water into rising vapor; that's where the cycle begins.
After vapor rises and the cloud forms, the droplets inside grow heavy and fall—which is the third stage, not the second.

problemText: A student claims: 'Once rain falls from a cloud onto the ground, that is the final stage and the water cycle is complete.' Is this claim correct or incorrect? Why or why not, in terms of the water cycle's four stages?
choices: The claim is correct because precipitation is the last stage, and once water reaches the ground the cycle stops.
The claim is incorrect because after precipitation, the water immediately evaporates back into the atmosphere, skipping any intermediate step between rainfall and the formation of new clouds.
The claim is incorrect because after precipitation, the water must undergo condensation again in order to form clouds and cycle back through the atmosphere rather than remaining on the ground.
The claim is incorrect because collection happens after precipitation, and collection returns water to lakes and oceans where evaporation can start the cycle again.
hints: Remember that the water cycle is a loop with no ending point—the fourth stage leads back to the first.
After rain falls (precipitation), water gathers into oceans, lakes, and rivers; that gathering is the stage that comes next.

problemText: A river flows into the ocean on the coast. A fish scientist tracks a single water droplet in that river as it enters the ocean and sits there for several weeks. Without external human interference, describe which four stages that droplet will move through next, in order, and explain why it returns to a location where the river cycle can begin again.
choices: Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection—the water evaporates from the ocean, condenses into a cloud, falls as rain, and collects in a river or lake where it can flow back to the ocean.
Collection, precipitation, condensation, evaporation—the water collects in the ocean, falls as rain, condenses into a cloud, and evaporates back into the ocean without ever returning to the river.
Condensation, precipitation, evaporation, collection—the water condenses as it sits in the ocean, falls as rain above the land, evaporates into the sky, and collects in rivers.
Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, evaporation—the water evaporates from the ocean, condenses twice into clouds, and falls as rain, then immediately evaporates again with no collection step.
hints: The four stages must happen in the same order every time: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection.
For the droplet to return to the river or a location where it can flow back to the ocean, it must be collected in a lake or river on land after it falls as precipitation.

problemText: A biome is defined by three key characteristics. Which set of three characteristics does a geographer use to identify and name a biome?
choices: Temperature, precipitation, and plant life
Elevation, rainfall, and animal species
Latitude, seasons, and forest density
Soil type, wind patterns, and tree height
hints: The lesson teaches that naming a biome requires reading all three clues together.
Think about what makes one biome different from another — the weather it has and what grows there.

problemText: A biome receives very little rain in every single month of the year. Most of the ground between plants is bare. Which biome does this description match?
choices: Rainforest
Desert
Tundra
Grassland
hints: The defining clue for one biome is very little precipitation all year — use that to narrow your choices.
Between desert and tundra, both are dry, so look at what covers the ground: is it bare or covered by mosses and shrubs?

problemText: A biome stays hot every single month of the year, with almost no change in temperature from season to season. Rain falls on most days, throughout the entire year. Which biome is this?
choices: Forest
Grassland
Rainforest
Desert
hints: The combination of constant heat and rain falling most days all year points to one biome.
Two biomes get enough rain to support many trees, but only one stays hot every single month with no cold season.

problemText: A student reads this description: 'Tall trees grow close together in layers. Only a few scattered trees stand far apart from each other.' The student says both describe the same biome because they both mention trees. Explain why the student is wrong, using at least one other clue besides plant life.
choices: The first describes a grassland with tall grasses and moderate rainfall; the second describes a rainforest with short plants on the forest floor and very high rainfall.
The first describes a forest with trees losing their leaves in winter and cooler temperatures; the second describes a grassland with evergreen trees that stay green year-round in a warmer climate.
The first describes a tundra where trees grow in layers and temperatures are very warm; the second describes a desert where trees are spaced far apart and temperatures are cold throughout the year.
The first describes a rainforest with dense, layered trees; the second describes a grassland with scattered trees because grasslands do not get enough rain to support many trees close together.
hints: Remember that forest and rainforest both grow many trees, and grassland also has scattered trees — so plant life alone cannot tell them apart.
Think about what separates grassland from rainforest: one does not get enough rain to support many trees close together, and one is not hot every single month.

problemText: Two places both have very little precipitation all year long. One has a ground covered in low mosses and small shrubs with no trees at all. The other has bare ground with only a few scattered plants widely spaced apart. Are these the same biome? Explain your answer using all three clues.
choices: No, they are different biomes: the first is a tundra with low mosses and shrubs covering the ground in a very cold place, and the second is a desert with bare ground between scattered plants in a hot place.

Yes, they are the same biome because both receive very little precipitation throughout the year, and lack of rain is the defining feature that overrides differences in temperature and plant density between regions.

No, they are different biomes: the first is a rainforest with dense plant cover that prevents bare ground from showing through, and the second is a grassland with scattered shrubs and exposed soil visible between patches of vegetation.

Yes, they are the same biome because both have very limited plant life with minimal coverage and low precipitation levels, which means both experience conditions too harsh to support tree growth of any kind in any season.
hints: Very low precipitation alone fits two different biomes in this lesson — you need to check temperature and plant life too.
A tundra is defined as cold, dry, and treeless, with mosses and shrubs covering the ground; a desert is defined as very dry with scattered plants and bare ground between them.

problemText: A biome has a warm part of the year and a genuinely cold part of the year, with enough precipitation spread throughout most of the year. Many trees grow close together there. Once the student identifies this as a forest using all three clues, the student then asks: 'If the temperature stayed the same but the precipitation changed to rain falling on most days all year with no dry season, would this still be a forest?' Using the three-clue method from the lesson, explain why or why not.
choices: No, because the addition of year-round rain with no dry season is the defining clue of a rainforest, and a rainforest stays hot every month with no cold season, so the plant life and precipitation clues would no longer match the forest's need for a cold season.

No, because very high precipitation with no dry season, combined with a hot temperature every month (since rainforests are hot), would switch the biome to rainforest, even though the temperature clue in the original forest description stays the same.
Yes, because both forest and rainforest have many trees growing close together, so adding more rain would not change the biome name.
Yes, because precipitation alone does not determine a biome — all three clues must change together for the biome name to change.
hints: Check what happens to the temperature clue if precipitation changes to year-round rain with no dry season: does a rainforest stay hot or cold every month?
The lesson shows that forest and rainforest are neighbors — forest needs a genuinely cold season, and rainforest needs to be hot every month, so changing one clue can flip which biome fits.

problemText: Which statement correctly defines what an ecosystem is?
choices: Only the plants and animals that live in a particular location
Every living and nonliving thing sharing one place, considered together
The smallest space where one specific animal makes its home
A group of living things that need the same type of food to survive
hints: Remember that an ecosystem includes both living AND nonliving parts.
Think about whether water, sunlight, and rocks are part of an ecosystem or not.

problemText: A student is looking at a backyard garden. She names these parts: soil, tomato plants, earthworms, rainwater, and a garden hose. Which of these is an abiotic (nonliving) part of the garden ecosystem?
choices: The tomato plants, because they stay rooted in one place
The earthworms, because they live in the soil
The rainwater, because it does not grow or reproduce
The garden hose, because it brings water from outside the garden
hints: Ask yourself: does this thing grow, need energy to survive, and make more of its own kind?
Look for something in the list that cannot do all three of those things.

problemText: A meadow ecosystem is described as: tall grass swaying in the wind, a rabbit hopping through the grass, morning sunlight warming the ground, insects flying low, and rich soil. Which choice correctly separates the biotic parts from the abiotic parts?
choices: Biotic: grass, rabbit, insects; Abiotic: wind, soil
Biotic: rabbit, insects, wind; Abiotic: grass, sunlight, soil
Biotic: grass, wind, insects; Abiotic: rabbit, sunlight, soil
Biotic: grass, rabbit, insects; Abiotic: sunlight, soil, wind
hints: Remember that wind is abiotic; it is not alive even though it moves things.
Use the three-part test: does it grow, need energy, and reproduce?

problemText: A student describes a forest this way: 'The whole forest is an ecosystem, but the fallen log covered with moss is a habitat.' Explain what the student got right and what the student got wrong about the forest.
choices: The student is right that the forest is the ecosystem and the log is a habitat inside it, but missed that many other habitats exist in the forest as well.

The student is right that the forest is an ecosystem, but wrong because the log is also a habitat and the forest itself is another habitat too, meaning multiple habitats can exist within one ecosystem.
The student is completely right; the forest is the ecosystem and the log is the only habitat inside it since habitats cannot overlap or share the same space.
The student is wrong about both parts; the fallen log is the ecosystem and the forest is one habitat within it, so habitats must contain ecosystems rather than the other way around.
hints: Think about whether one ecosystem can hold more than one habitat at the same time.
Ask: can different animals live in different spots inside the forest, each in their own habitat?

problemText: A student says: 'A beach is not an ecosystem because it is mostly made of sand, which is nonliving.' What is the error in this reasoning, and why is the student wrong?
choices: The student is wrong because an ecosystem must include only living things and exclude all nonliving materials, so the presence of sand actually means the beach cannot qualify as a true ecosystem.
The student is wrong because an ecosystem needs BOTH living and nonliving parts together; the sand is abiotic, but if crabs, seaweed, and shells are also there, the beach is still a full ecosystem.

The student is wrong because ecosystems are defined as containing only the living parts of a place, not the nonliving parts, which means sand and water should be counted separately from the organisms.
The student is wrong because ecosystems require exactly equal amounts of living and nonliving things to be present, and beaches fail to meet this balance requirement since sand dominates.
hints: Remember the definition of ecosystem: BOTH living AND nonliving parts sharing one place.
Think about whether a beach would have any living things on or in it.

problemText: Two students visit a tide pool during low tide. One student says: 'This tide pool is a habitat, not an ecosystem, because it is too small.' The other student says: 'The tide pool is an ecosystem because it has starfish, seaweed, rocks, seawater, and sunlight all in one place.' Who is correct, and why? What mistake did the first student make in understanding the difference between ecosystem and habitat?
choices: The first student is correct; any place smaller than a mile across is only a habitat and cannot be called an ecosystem. The second student confused the depth of water with the number of different species present.

The first student is correct; a tide pool has too many living things to be a habitat and too few organisms to be an ecosystem. The second student forgot that ecosystems require both rocks and water to be counted.

The second student is correct; the tide pool is an ecosystem with all living and nonliving parts together. The first student mistakenly thought that habitat and ecosystem mean the same thing, or that size alone decides which is which.

The second student is correct; the tide pool is an ecosystem because it has living things and nonliving parts working together in one location. The first student confused the size of a space with whether it could contain a complete ecosystem.
hints: Recall: an ecosystem is EVERY living and nonliving thing in one place; a habitat is the specific spot where ONE particular living thing lives.
Size does not determine whether something is an ecosystem or habitat. What matters is whether you are describing the whole system or just one small spot inside it.
